evaluated.name: FundingQueuePosition
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(IND_ADJ(RATIO(ADD(ADD(capx, aqc), ADD(dlc, dvc)), ADD(che, ppent))), 1)), ZSCORE(SUB(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(ADD(capx, aqc), ADD(dlc, dvc)), ADD(che, ppent)), 1), IND_ADJ(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(ADD(capx, aqc), ADD(dlc, dvc)), ADD(che, ppent)), 1)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Capital is allocated competitively within industries: being the worst-funded firm in an industry whose peers are all stretched means standing last in the queue for scarce external capital, whereas the same absolute funding gap in an industry where rivals are cash-rich can be financed on ordinary terms.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the anomaly bundle with a genuinely cross-level mechanism — the firm's rank within its industry's funding distribution multiplied by that industry's own average funding stress, recovered as the difference between the raw and industry-adjusted measure — so the score identifies relative position in a competition for capital rather than any single firm characteristic. It differs from the earlier hot-issuance-wave test both in the state variable (total funding coverage rather than issuance activity) and in its long tail, which is well-funded firms inside comfortable industries, the population that has carried the correct side of every successful signal in this archive.
evaluated.author: proposer

considered.name: PersistentExternallyFundedExpansion
considered.expression: MUL(TS_SUM(RATIO(ADD(capx, aqc), at), 3), TS_SUM(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(sstk, dltis), ADD(prstkc, dltr)), at), 1), 3))
considered.hypothesis: Multi-year investment programs continuously refinanced by external capital markets reflect entrenched empire building, whereas a single year of externally funded capex can be lumpy but value-creating.
considered.reasoning: The product of a three-year cumulative investment rate and a three-year cumulative net external financing rate is large only for firms that repeatedly spend and repeatedly raise, capturing a persistent state rather than a one-off transaction. Smoothing both legs also reduces the annual-report noise that weakens contemporaneous interaction sorts.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: IssuanceInvestmentMismatch
considered.expression: SUB(IND_RANK(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at)), IND_RANK(RATIO(ADD(capx, aqc), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Capital raised in excess of what the firm actually deploys into investment is the purest evidence of opportunistic market timing; matched issuance-and-investment is much less informative because the money has an identified use.
considered.reasoning: Differencing industry ranks of gross external issuance and gross investment isolates the wedge between funds raised and funds spent, so the extreme short leg contains issuers with no corresponding real spending. It is a mismatch (orthogonalized) interaction rather than a product, and therefore captures a distinct part of the investment-financing joint distribution from Signals 1-4.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: DualMarketFundedGrowth
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 1)), MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(sstk, at)), IND_RANK(RATIO(dltis, at))))
considered.hypothesis: Expansion that requires a firm to tap equity and debt markets *simultaneously* is the clearest sign that internal resources and a single funding channel were insufficient, so it reflects capital-market-enabled overexpansion rather than opportunity-driven growth.
considered.reasoning: Replacing the zero/one indicator with the product of non-negative industry ranks makes the score monotone in both legs: the short leg is unambiguously high-growth firms drawing on both markets, and the long leg is slow-growing firms that raised little of either kind of capital, so the externally funded shrinkers that contaminated the original long leg no longer sit there. The MIN operator is what separates this from the published net-external-financing composite, where large debt issuance can substitute for equity issuance in a sum; here a firm scores high only if *both* markets are being used at once.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: StockSwapIntangibleExpansion
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(intan, 1), LAG(at, 1)), 1)), SUMRANK(RATIO(sstk, at), WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Deals paid for with the firm's own paper leave a balance-sheet footprint (a jump in goodwill and other intangibles plus a jump in shares outstanding) without a matching cash outflow, and this paper-funded expansion signals managerial belief that the equity is overvalued.
considered.reasoning: This fixes the measurement error the critic identified: cash-acquisition spend (aqc) is dropped entirely and deal activity is measured by the growth in total intangibles, which rises for stock-swap deals precisely because no cash leaves the firm. The consideration channel is proxied by two complementary issuance measures combined with SUMRANK, so a share count inflated by a split (which does not raise sstk) or an equity raise held as cash (which does not grow intangibles) cannot by itself place a firm in the short leg; both legs are non-negative ranks, so the score is monotone.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: LeveredCapacityBuild
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(ppegt, 1), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(dltis, dltr), LAG(at, 1)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Gross capacity added with newly borrowed money creates committed fixed costs and inflexible, hard-to-reverse assets, so these firms underperform once the capacity fails to earn its cost of capital; identical capacity growth funded without new debt carries no such burden.
considered.reasoning: Ranking PP&E growth before multiplying removes the sign flip the critic flagged: shrinking-asset borrowers now receive a low PP&E-growth rank and therefore a low, not extreme-negative, score, so they no longer populate the leg that is supposed to hold conservative firms. Both inputs are non-negative industry ranks, so the score rises monotonically in capacity growth and in *net* debt raised (issuance minus retirement, rather than the change in debt balances, which mixes in reclassification and currency effects), and the short leg is unambiguously the levered capacity builder.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PayoutFundedInvestment
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, LAG(ppent, 1)), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), ADD(sstk, dltis)), at), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Firms that invest heavily in their installed base while simultaneously distributing cash to shareholders and repaying capital providers are investing out of genuine internal cash generation, and this self-funded investment earns higher subsequent returns than externally funded investment of the same size.
considered.reasoning: The signed z-score product is replaced by the product of two non-negative industry ranks, which removes the ambiguity the critic identified: a low-investment heavy issuer now scores near zero on both legs rather than mimicking the high-investment payer, so only firms that are jointly high-investment and net distributors sit in the long leg. The financing leg is a payout-minus-issuance intensity (repurchases plus dividends less equity and debt issues), so the interaction explicitly tests investment conditional on the firm being a net supplier rather than consumer of external capital.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: NonCashDealExpansion
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(intan, 1), aqc), LAG(at, 1)), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Intangible and goodwill growth that is *not* matched by cash acquisition outlays must have been paid for in paper, and paper-funded expansion signals that management is exploiting an overvalued equity price.
considered.reasoning: This sharpens the batch's best portfolio performer by subtracting cash acquisition spend from intangible growth, so the investment leg now measures the specifically non-cash-funded part of deal-driven expansion rather than all intangible growth. The consideration leg switches from sstk to share-count growth, which is available for nearly every firm-year, addressing the low coverage that made the original's deciles thin.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: DeleveragingInvestor
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, LAG(ppent, 1)), 1)), SUMRANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(lt, at), 1)), RATIO(dvc, at)))
considered.hypothesis: Investing heavily while simultaneously reducing leverage and paying dividends is only possible out of genuine internal cash generation, and this self-funded investment should earn higher subsequent risk-adjusted returns than externally funded investment of comparable size.
considered.reasoning: PayoutFundedInvestment had the right sign but weak precision (fmb 1.84, ls_talpha 1.53), plausibly because its financing leg relied on sparse repurchase and issuance flows; here the funding-source leg is built from the change in the liability-to-asset ratio and the dividend rate, both nearly universally available. Both factors are non-negative ranks, so the long leg is unambiguously the high-investment deleveraging dividend payer and the short leg is low-investment firms levering up.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: IssuedAndSpentVersusHoarded
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, LAG(ppent, 1)), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(che, 1), LAG(at, 1)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: New equity that is immediately converted into physical investment reveals overinvestment, whereas new equity parked in cash is a precautionary buffer that carries no such penalty and may even predict higher returns.
considered.reasoning: This directly confronts the critic's Palazzo objection to the accepted mismatch signal by separating the deployment of raised capital from its retention: the second factor is positive only when issuance exceeds cash accumulation, so the interaction shorts high-capex issuers who spent the money and goes long high-capex firms building cash without issuing. It tests whether the pricing consequence of external financing depends on where the money went, a conditioning dimension no prior proposal in the archive addresses.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CapexFundingMixTilt
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, LAG(ppegt, 1)), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(lt, 1), capx), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: For a given rate of capital spending, the source of the money is what predicts returns: each dollar of capex backed by newly raised outside claims reflects an expansion the firm could not fund itself, whereas capex covered by internal resources is a positive signal.
considered.reasoning: The financing leg is now a funding *mix* — liability dollars raised per dollar of capital spending, industry-demeaned and signed — rather than a level of debt growth, so scaling investment and financing up together leaves the score unchanged and the construct cannot be a restatement of asset growth or of the debt-issuance anomaly. The non-negative capex-rate rank acts purely as an exposure weight: low investors score near zero regardless of funding mix, while heavy investors are sorted by whether the program was outside-funded (short leg) or self-funded (long leg), which is the interaction the theme asks for.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: LaborTiltedExternallyFundedScaling
considered.expression: MUL(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(GROWTH(emp, 1), GROWTH(ppent, 1)), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Firms that scale headcount far faster than their capital base while issuing equity are building organizational overhead on outside money rather than productive capacity, and this asset-light externally funded scaling is where expansion disappoints.
considered.reasoning: Netting PP&E growth out of employment growth removes the part of the hiring rate that is common to the published employment-growth and asset-growth anomalies, so the surviving investment leg is a labor-versus-capital *tilt* with mean zero within industry rather than a growth level. Because that tilt is signed and is multiplied by the issuance rank, non-issuers land near zero and the sort contrasts labor-tilted issuers (short) against capital-tilted issuers (long) — a comparison that cannot be produced by adding two negative main effects.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: TradeCreditFundedInventory
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(invt, 1), LAG(at, 1)), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(SUB(lt, dltt), 1), DELTA(che, 1)), LAG(at, 1)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Inventory accumulation is benign when the firm pays for it out of its own cash, but signals unsold goods plus a liquidity squeeze when it is carried on payables and short-term credit while cash is not drawn down.
considered.reasoning: The financing leg is rebuilt as total liabilities less long-term debt, which is genuinely current liabilities including payables — this both removes the Δdlc double count the critic identified and delivers the trade-credit content the hypothesis claimed. Adding the change in cash makes the leg a funding-source contrast rather than a growth level: it is high only when short-term outside claims expand *without* internal cash being spent, and because that leg is signed and industry-demeaned the product separates externally financed inventory builds (short) from self-funded ones (long) instead of collapsing onto inventory or asset growth.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: DealDeploymentVersusHoarding
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(aqc, DELTA(intan, 1)), LAG(at, 1)), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(che, 1), LAG(at, 1)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: The overvaluation content of external financing depends on whether the money is converted into acquired businesses and intangibles or retained as cash; deal-driven external growth is the empire-building case, cash retention is precautionary.
considered.reasoning: This holds the winning conditioning structure fixed and swaps the investment channel from organic capex to inorganic expansion (cash acquisitions plus intangible additions), which is the cleanest way to learn whether the deploy-versus-hoard dimension is a general funding-source effect or specific to capital spending. It also directly reuses the diagnostic that intangible/deal growth interacted with issuance gave the strongest FMB slopes in the archive but no aligned portfolio alpha when built as a non-negative rank product.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PeakInvestmentOnOutsideMoney
considered.expression: MUL(TS_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, LAG(ppent, 1)), 1), 5), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(GROWTH(csho, 1), RATIO(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), LAG(at, 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: What matters is not whether a firm invests a lot relative to peers but whether it is at the top of its own investment cycle while leaning on capital markets — cyclical peak spending financed externally is where extrapolative overinvestment concentrates.
considered.reasoning: TS_RANK places the current capex rate in the firm's own five-year history, removing the cross-sectional capex-intensity level that plausibly drives most of the FF5 alpha in the two archive signals sharing a capex leg, so a result here would be genuinely incremental to the investment main effect. The financing leg is an industry-demeaned signed combination of share-count growth and debt growth, so peak investors funding internally take the opposite tail rather than clustering at zero.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: BorrowedVersusHoardedAcquisitions
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(aqc, LAG(at, 1)), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), LAG(at, 1)), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(DELTA(che, 1), LAG(at, 1))), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Cash acquisitions funded by fresh borrowing reflect managers stretching for scale beyond internal means, whereas identical-sized deals paid out of an accumulated cash war chest reflect pre-funded, discretionary investment and should not be penalized.
considered.reasoning: This separates two funding routes for the *same* real action, which is the sharpest possible test of the theme and is unavailable in the capex channel because capex is rarely traceable to a single source. The contrast leg ranks new debt against cash drawdown, so both tails are heavy acquirers and the sort cannot be a restatement of acquisition intensity or of the debt-growth main effect.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: SerialIssuerInvestmentProgram
considered.expression: MUL(TS_SUM(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, LAG(ppent, 1)), 1), 3), SUB(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 0.02), 3), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(RATIO(dvc, at), 0.005), 3)))
considered.hypothesis: Repetition is what distinguishes empire building from lumpy investment: a firm that has funded a multi-year investment program by returning to shareholders for new capital year after year, never paying a dividend, is systematically overextending, while a firm running the same program while paying dividends every year is self-financing.
considered.reasoning: The financing leg counts *how many* of the past three years featured meaningful share issuance versus a dividend, turning funding source into a persistence state rather than a one-year flow, which is a dimension no archive signal captures except through smoothed level sums that produced no portfolio alpha. Differencing the two counts keeps the score signed and centred, so persistent investors split into repeat-issuer and repeat-payer tails instead of stacking monotonically with cumulative investment.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: DeployingLastYearsRaise
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(capx, LAG(ppent, 1)), 1), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(LAG(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1), LAG(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), LAG(at, 1)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Capital is raised before it is spent, and the mispricing is resolved during the deployment stage: firms that ramp up capital spending this year using money raised from markets last year are the ones whose expansion plans were validated only by cheap external capital, not by internal cash generation.
considered.reasoning: The mechanism is the sequencing of the funding cycle rather than the contemporaneous funding mix, so the investment leg is the *change* in the capex rate (the ramp) and the financing leg is prior-year external funding, a combination no archive signal contains and which cannot be a reparameterization of PayoutFundedInvestment or the mismatch family. The financing leg is industry-demeaned and signed, so firms ramping investment without a prior raise take the opposite tail, and the lag structure also means the signal is measured after issuance-window effects have largely passed.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: MaturityMismatchedCapacityFunding
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(ppegt, 1), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(lt, dltt), 1), LAG(at, 1)), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(dltt, 1), LAG(at, 1)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Funding long-lived, irreversible physical capacity with short-dated claims (payables and current debt) rather than term debt creates rollover and refinancing risk that must be resolved by fire sales or dilution, so duration-mismatched expansion underperforms duration-matched expansion of identical size.
considered.reasoning: This changes the financing dimension from *how much* outside money was raised to *what maturity* it carries, an independent, theory-driven prediction (duration matching, Diamond-style rollover risk) rather than a sign inherited from any in-sample result. The contrast leg ranks short-dated liability growth against long-term debt growth so both tails are heavy capacity builders, isolating funding structure rather than expansion magnitude, and it uses only universally reported balance-sheet items so coverage stays at the high end of the archive.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: InvestmentBeyondInternalLiquidity
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(capx, aqc), LAG(at, 1)), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(che, LAG(at, 1)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Equity issuance is benign for a firm whose cash reserves already cover its investment program and toxic for a firm whose spending plans far exceed its liquid resources, because only the latter must keep returning to the market on whatever terms it can get.
considered.reasoning: This reverses the roles of the two legs relative to the champion: issuance becomes the exposure weight and the contrast measures the *stock* gap between the investment program and the liquidity buffer, which is a firm-level external-finance-dependence measure rather than a flow. It directly engages the Palazzo objection the critic raised, since the long tail is issuers sitting on large cash relative to modest investment, exactly the firms cash-holdings evidence says should earn high returns.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: FundedInvestmentRampVersusOwnNorm
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(capx, LAG(ppent, 1)), MA(RATIO(capx, LAG(ppent, 1)), 3)), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(che, 1), LAG(at, 1)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Overinvestment shows up as a firm spending abnormally relative to its own recent norm while simultaneously spending fresh outside capital; a firm at its usual investment rate, or one that banked the money it raised, has not overextended.
considered.reasoning: PeakInvestmentOnOutsideMoney had the strongest FMB slope in the archive (-4.76) but no alpha, and its two suspects are a five-valued TS_RANK weight and a z-score financing leg; this replaces the first with a continuous deviation from the firm's own three-year average capex rate and the second with the deploy-versus-hoard rank contrast that has demonstrated portfolio traction. If it works, it shows the within-firm timing insight was real and only the portfolio construction was broken, which is a genuinely diagnostic outcome.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: UnstablyFundedInvestment
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, LAG(ppent, 1)), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(VOL(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1), 5)), IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(dvc, at), 3))))
considered.hypothesis: Long-lived investment programs financed by an erratic, stop-start stream of equity issuance are fragile — the firm cannot commit to completing them — whereas the same programs financed by the steady internal cash flow evidenced by a stable dividend are sustainable.
considered.reasoning: Every archive signal characterizes funding by its level or sign; none uses the *second moment* of the funding stream, yet financing volatility is precisely what distinguishes an opportunistic serial issuer from a firm with a reliable funding plan. The contrast subtracts a smoothed dividend rate so the long tail is heavy investors with steady internal funding and the short tail is heavy investors with volatile market funding, keeping the sort two-tailed within the high-investment group.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: HotIssuanceMarketInvestor
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, LAG(ppent, 1)), 1)), ZSCORE(SUB(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1), IND_ADJ(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: Aggressive investment is most damaging when the firm's whole industry is being flooded with new equity, because industry-wide cheap capital produces capacity gluts and competitive dissipation of returns; the same investment rate in an industry where no one can raise money reflects genuine advantage.
considered.reasoning: Subtracting the industry-adjusted value from the raw value recovers the *industry-year mean* issuance rate, so the financing leg is a market-condition variable rather than another firm-level anomaly leg — this is a cross-level interaction (firm investment × industry funding climate) that no archive signal contains and that cannot be a re-parameterization of IssuedAndSpentVersusHoarded. Because the industry wave term is cross-sectionally standardized and signed, heavy investors in cold-financing industries occupy the long tail while heavy investors in hot-issuance industries occupy the short tail, keeping the sort two-tailed rather than monotone in expansion.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PeckingOrderViolationInvestment
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, LAG(ppent, 1)), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(lt, at), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: A heavy investor that issues equity while its balance sheet still has ample unused debt capacity is violating the pecking order, and the only coherent reason to prefer expensive equity over cheap debt is that management thinks the shares are overpriced; a heavy investor that is already highly levered issues equity out of necessity, not opportunism.
considered.reasoning: The critic is right that differencing two same-signed anomalies is unmotivated, so the debt leg is replaced by the *level* of leverage, which theory and evidence associate with higher — not lower — expected returns, meaning the long tail (levered, non-issuing investors) is no longer stacked with a known negative predictor. The score therefore identifies the specific pecking-order violation that reveals market timing, and both tails remain heavy investors so the sort is a funding-choice comparison rather than an investment-intensity sort.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PaperFundedRollUp
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(gdwl, at), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dvc, prstkc), at), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: A large accumulated stock of acquisition goodwill is only a warning when the firm is still funding itself by issuing shares rather than returning cash: the ongoing paper-funded roll-up is where promised synergies fail and impairments follow, while the same goodwill stock at a firm now paying dividends and buying back stock represents digested, completed deals.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the arithmetically degenerate per-share growth construct and instead interacts a *stock* of past externally funded expansion (goodwill on the balance sheet) with the firm's *current* funding posture, a state-times-behaviour combination absent from the archive and immune to the split-adjustment problem since share growth enters only as a cross-sectional rank. The signed payout-versus-issuance contrast makes the two tails equally goodwill-heavy, so the sort compares live roll-ups against consolidated acquirers rather than restating the intangible-growth or issuance main effects.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ProceedsToInvestmentVersusDebtRetirement
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(capx, aqc), LAG(at, 1)), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(dltr, LAG(at, 1)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Equity raised and pushed into new assets is empire building, whereas equity raised to retire debt is a balance-sheet repair that transfers value to shareholders from creditors and leaves no new capacity to disappoint.
considered.reasoning: The archive has tested two destinations for raised capital — real investment and the cash account — but never debt retirement, which is economically the opposite of expansion and is the classic recapitalization use of proceeds. Holding the issuance weight fixed and contrasting the two destinations keeps both tails populated by issuers, so the sort identifies use of proceeds rather than the issuance anomaly itself.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PayoutCutFundedInvestmentRamp
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(capx, LAG(ppent, 1)), 1), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(dvt, at), 1)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Managers can fund expansion by quietly withholding cash from shareholders instead of going to markets; an investment ramp financed by a shrinking payout escapes both market scrutiny and creditor screening and is the least disciplined form of expansion.
considered.reasoning: Every archive entry treats internal funding as the benign pole, but payout reduction is an internal funding source that carries the opposite governance implication from retained cash flow, so this tests whether "self-funded" is really benign or merely unmonitored. The financing leg is a signed industry-standardized change in the payout rate, so firms ramping investment while raising payout occupy the long tail, giving a two-sided sort along a channel no prior signal touches.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ForcedIssuanceAtLiquidityTrough
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, LAG(ppent, 1)), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1)), TS_RANK(RATIO(che, at), 5)))
considered.hypothesis: Issuing equity when the firm's own liquidity has fallen to the bottom of its five-year range is forced financing on the market's terms, while issuing from the top of its liquidity range is opportunistic and discretionary; only the forced case reveals that the investment program has outrun the firm's capacity to fund it.
considered.reasoning: Cross-sectional cash levels conflate industry norms and business models, whereas the firm's position within its own liquidity history measures whether the buffer is genuinely depleted — the same within-firm reframing that turned a flat-alpha signal into a working one in gen 3. Both legs are bounded in [0,1] so the contrast is well scaled, and heavy investors at their liquidity peak occupy the long tail rather than being pooled at zero.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: WorkingCapitalReleaseFundedRamp
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(capx, LAG(ppent, 1)), 1), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(DELTA(invt, 1), LAG(at, 1))), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: A firm that steps up capital spending by squeezing cash out of its own working capital is reallocating internally under operating discipline, whereas a firm that funds the identical step-up by issuing shares has bought growth with other people's money; the first expansion is validated by the business, the second only by the share price.
considered.reasoning: Working capital has appeared in the archive only as a *use* of funds (TradeCreditFundedInventory); treating inventory liquidation as a *source* of funds for an investment ramp is a new economic channel and the only internal funding source that is observable without any income-statement input. The contrast is signed and both tails are firms ramping investment, so the sort compares two funding routes for the same real action rather than restating the inventory-growth or issuance main effects.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: SelfFundedVersusMarketFundedGate
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, LAG(ppent, 1)), 1)), SIGN(SUB(IND_RANK(RATIO(dvc, at)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: The identical investment rate carries opposite information depending on the funding regime: for a firm that returns more cash to shareholders than it takes from them, heavy investment signals profitable opportunities, while for a firm that is a net taker of shareholder capital the same heavy investment signals overvaluation-driven expansion.
considered.reasoning: This uses a hard sign gate rather than a graded rank difference, which is a structurally different conditioning device from anything in the archive: the score is +capex-rank for net-payer firms and −capex-rank for net-taker firms, so both extreme deciles are heavy investors and the spread is a pure funding-regime contrast with the investment main effect differenced out. The direction is supported independently of any single prior result — PayoutFundedInvestment (fmb +1.84, alpha +1.7%) and IssuedAndSpentVersusHoarded (alpha -2.5% for the spending issuers) both point to payers being the good side within high investors.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: BorrowedVersusWarChestAcquisitions
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(aqc, LAG(at, 1)), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(dltis, LAG(at, 1)), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(DELTA(che, 1), LAG(at, 1))), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Cash acquisitions financed by fresh borrowing reflect managers stretching beyond internal means and pushing repayment risk onto the future, whereas identically sized deals paid out of a previously accumulated cash reserve reflect pre-funded, discretionary capital allocation.
considered.reasoning: This tests the funding source of one narrowly defined real action and has never been evaluated — the earlier version failed validation for lacking a financing-exclusive variable, which long-term debt issuance now supplies — and it is unrelated to the stock-swap literature because aqc captures cash deals only. Both tails are heavy cash acquirers, so the comparison is borrowing versus war-chest drawdown rather than an acquisition-intensity or debt-issuance sort; the acknowledged risk is that cash drawdown partly proxies for operating burn, which the acquisition-intensity weight mitigates by restricting attention to firms actually buying assets.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: NetShareholderCapitalDependence
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sstk, ADD(prstkc, dvc)), LAG(at, 1)), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(capx, aqc), LAG(at, 1)), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(che, LAG(at, 1)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Dependence on shareholder capital is a continuum from large net returner to large net taker, and the return penalty for running an investment program that exceeds internal liquidity should scale monotonically along that continuum rather than switching on only for share issuers.
considered.reasoning: The archive's largest alpha (-5.3%, t -5.60) came with a flat FMB slope (-0.70), and the mechanical reason is that its weight was gross share-count growth, which is bunched near its lower bound for the roughly half of the cross-section that neither issues nor buys back, leaving the interaction undefined through the middle of the distribution. Replacing it with net shareholder capital flow (issues less repurchases and dividends) gives the weight full support in both directions without altering the mechanism, which is the specific design choice needed to convert tail strength into a cross-sectional slope.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: FinancingChurnInvestor
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, LAG(ppent, 1)), 1)), MIN(IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1)), IND_RANK(RATIO(ADD(dvc, prstkc), at))))
considered.hypothesis: A firm that takes capital from shareholders and simultaneously hands capital back while investing heavily has no coherent funding plan; this churn is a symptom of managers who will not subordinate distributions to their own investment program, and it signals weak capital discipline rather than either genuine self-funding or clean market funding.
considered.reasoning: Every archive construction treats raising and returning capital as opposite poles of one axis, so the case where both are large simultaneously has never been isolated; MIN is the natural operator for "both at once" and has not been used in any prior entry. The high tail is heavy investors who are round-tripping shareholder capital, the low tail is heavy investors doing neither, so the score is orthogonal by construction to the net-financing measures that dominate the archive.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: YoungBaseExternallyFundedExpansion
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ppent, ppegt), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1)), IND_RANK(RATIO(dvc, at))))
considered.hypothesis: Externally funded investment is defensible when it replaces a worn-out asset base and suspicious when the existing base is already new: a firm whose plant is largely undepreciated yet keeps raising shareholder capital instead of distributing it is adding capacity the business does not need to maintain.
considered.reasoning: The ratio of net to gross PP&E is a clean vintage measure that separates replacement investment from genuine expansion, a distinction the archive has never made even though it is central to whether spending is value-neutral maintenance or discretionary empire building. Because the vintage weight is a level and the funding leg is a signed issuance-versus-payout contrast, both tails are young-asset-base firms and the sort cannot restate the investment-growth or issuance main effects.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: DilutionWithoutCapitalAccumulation
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, LAG(ppent, 1)), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(ceq, at), 1), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Issuing shares while the equity cushion per unit of assets is shrinking means the new capital is being consumed as fast as it arrives, so existing owners are diluted without the firm's capital base growing; a heavy investor whose equity share of assets is rising without dilution is funding itself out of retained value.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the financing-deficit identity the critic correctly identified as net external financing and instead measures whether shareholder dilution is accompanied by any accumulation of the equity claim, a stock-versus-flow inconsistency that no archive entry examines and that is not the issuance anomaly (issuers whose equity ratio climbs land in the opposite tail). Both tails are heavy investors, so the sort prices how the expansion was capitalized rather than the level of investment or of issuance.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: WideningFundingDependenceTrend
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(TREND(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, LAG(ppent, 1)), 1), 5)), IND_ZSCORE(TREND(WINSOR(RATIO(lt, at), 1), 5)))
considered.hypothesis: Externally funded empire building is a multi-year trajectory rather than a single transaction: a firm whose investment intensity has been trending up for years while its claim structure has been trending steadily more levered is on an unsustainable path, whereas a firm ramping investment while its liability share trends down is financing expansion out of accumulating internal value.
considered.reasoning: Every archive entry uses one-year flows, three-year sums, or a deviation from a moving average; none uses the slope of the two themes' trajectories, yet the distinction between a firm drifting into dependence and one making a single lumpy raise is exactly what the empire-building story requires. The financing trend is industry-standardized and signed so deleveraging investors take the long tail, and both legs are slow-moving states, which should give more stable portfolio composition than the flow-based entries whose deciles turn over annually.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: BorrowingWhileRetrenching
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(lt, 1), LAG(at, 1)), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(capx, LAG(ppent, 1)), 1)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Outside money raised while investment is being cut is not funding growth at all — it is absorbing operating shortfalls and working-capital drains — and this "borrowing to survive" pattern is a more reliable warning than borrowing to expand, because the firm is adding fixed claims without adding any earning assets.
considered.reasoning: The archive has tested only the empire-building corner of the investment-financing plane, where funding and spending rise together; this proposal prices the opposite corner, where liabilities rise as spending falls, which is a distress mechanism rather than an overvaluation mechanism and therefore a genuinely new economic channel rather than a leg swap. The financing weight is non-negative and the investment leg is a signed change, so heavy borrowers who are simultaneously accelerating investment occupy the long tail, isolating the retrenchment interaction rather than the debt-growth main effect.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CollateralPoorDependence
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(intan, at), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(che, LAG(at, 1)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Market dependence bites hardest where the asset base cannot be pledged: an intangible-heavy firm that is issuing equity from a thin cash position has no collateral to fall back on if capital markets close, whereas a tangible-asset firm in the same funding position retains borrowing capacity.
considered.reasoning: The archive has weighted the funding-versus-liquidity contrast by investment intensity, deal intensity, asset vintage and issuance, but never by asset *pledgeability*, which is the variable that determines whether external dependence is a real constraint or a choice. Both tails are intangible-heavy firms, so the sort prices funding fragility conditional on collateral rather than restating the intangible-intensity or issuance effects.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: SupplierFundedCapex
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, LAG(ppent, 1)), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(lt, ADD(dltt, dlc)), 1), LAG(at, 1)), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(che, LAG(at, 1)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Firms that fund fixed-asset programs by stretching suppliers and accruing unpaid obligations are using the least visible and least patient form of outside money; this hidden leverage is a warning that neither internal cash nor formal capital markets were available.
considered.reasoning: Total liabilities net of all interest-bearing debt isolates operating creditors and accruals, a funding source the archive has touched only for inventory (TradeCreditFundedInventory, which produced a wrong-signed alpha because its financing leg mixed cash and short-term debt) and never for capital spending. Contrasting that source against the cash buffer keeps the alpha-carrying liquidity dimension while the mechanism — supplier-financed capacity — is economically distinct from equity or debt issuance.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: TripleHurdleMarketDependence
considered.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(capx, aqc), LAG(at, 1)), 1)), MIN(IND_RANK(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(che, LAG(at, 1))), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: The externally funded expansion story requires three conditions at once — a large program, no internal liquidity, and actual recourse to shareholders — and firms satisfying all three simultaneously are the population where overvaluation-driven expansion is unambiguous.
considered.reasoning: The rank-difference implementation of this idea produced a huge alpha but no cross-sectional slope because a high score can be earned two different ways (big program, or tiny cash balance), whereas the nested MIN scores a firm only as high as its weakest condition, making the measure monotone in genuine joint dependence. It is a structural rather than cosmetic change to the archive's best-performing population, and the long tail — firms failing any one hurdle — is economically well defined rather than a mixture of opposite types.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: UncoveredShareOfProgram
considered.expression: IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(capx, aqc), ADD(ADD(capx, aqc), ADD(che, ADD(dvc, prstkc)))), 1))
considered.hypothesis: The economically meaningful quantity is the fraction of a firm's investment program that its own resources cannot cover: as the cash balance and the distributions management chose to make shrink relative to spending, the share of the program that must come from outside investors approaches one, and that uncovered share is what predicts low returns.
considered.reasoning: Putting the program in both the numerator and the denominator bounds the measure in the unit interval, which removes the hyperbolic 1/cash behaviour the critic identified while preserving the same economics — a firm with resources far exceeding its program sits near zero, a firm with no resources sits near one, and winsorization no longer performs the ordering. The two themes remain inseparable in the construct (investment in the numerator, internal financing capacity in the denominator), and it is monotone by design, which is what the flat FMB slopes of the rank-difference versions were lacking.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: RealizedVersusLatentDependence
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(capx, aqc), ADD(ADD(capx, aqc), ADD(che, ADD(dvc, prstkc)))), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sstk, prstkc), LAG(at, 1)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Having an investment program that exceeds internal resources is only a warning if the firm actually acted on it: a structurally dependent firm that went to shareholders for net new capital has confirmed the gap, while an equally dependent firm that instead bought back stock must have had funding capacity the balance sheet does not show.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the level-plus-momentum construction the critic objected to with a latent-versus-realized distinction: the bounded uncovered-share measure identifies who *needs* outside money and the signed net equity flow identifies who *took* it, so the interaction separates confirmed dependence from apparent dependence. Because the financing leg is signed and centred, dependent repurchasers occupy the long tail and non-dependent firms cluster near zero regardless of their issuance, which keeps the sort focused on the interaction rather than on the issuance main effect.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: NearTermObligationsDuringExpansion
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, LAG(ppent, 1)), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(dlc, LAG(at, 1)), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(che, dvc), LAG(at, 1)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: A firm investing heavily with more debt maturing inside a year than it holds in cash and discretionary dividends must refinance while it is still spending, so its expansion depends on continuous market access; an equally aggressive investor whose maturing debt is covered by liquid resources can complete the program regardless of market conditions.
considered.reasoning: The obligation leg is now purely forward-looking — debt in current liabilities, which is contractually due within the year — with the backward-looking repayment flow removed, so the measure is genuinely a refinancing wall rather than a mixture of a stock and a realized outflow. The buffer side adds the dividend to cash because a payment management can suspend is a real source of liquidity, making the contrast a coverage test; both tails are heavy investors, so the sort isolates refinancing exposure rather than leverage or investment intensity.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: OutsideFundingBreadthCapex
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, LAG(ppent, 1)), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(lt, ADD(dltt, dlc)), 1), LAG(at, 1)), GROWTH(csho, 1))), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(che, LAG(at, 1)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Non-interest-bearing operating credit and new equity are both outside money that a capital-spending firm can lean on, and a firm funding its program from either while holding no liquid buffer is dependent regardless of which of the two it used.
considered.reasoning: SupplierFundedCapex delivered a strong alpha (-3.1%, t -3.35) but a weak slope (-1.57), and the natural diagnosis is that operating-liability growth alone is a narrow, noisy funding channel; pooling it with equity issuance broadens the funding leg without abandoning the supplier-credit insight. This also partially addresses the critic's concern that the leg is a pure operating-liability sort, since a firm scoring high must be short of cash while funded from at least one outside source.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ChronicDependenceCount
considered.expression: TS_SUM(MIN(INDICATOR(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1), 0.02), INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(ADD(capx, aqc), LAG(at, 1)), RATIO(che, LAG(at, 1))), 0)), 3)
considered.hypothesis: Being externally dependent for one year can be a lumpy project; being dependent for three years running is a business model, and chronic dependence identifies firms whose expansion has never been validated by internally generated resources.
considered.reasoning: The archive measures the dependent state only contemporaneously; this counts how many of the last three years the firm was simultaneously issuing equity and running an investment program larger than its cash balance, using MIN as a logical AND on the two indicators. It is a discrete, slow-moving state variable, which should give far more stable portfolio composition than the annual-flow constructions whose deciles turn over every year, and its long tail is firms that have never been in the dependent state.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: BorrowingHeadroomDependence
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(ppent, lt)), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(che, LAG(at, 1)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: What makes market dependence bite is having no debt capacity left: a firm whose pledgeable plant is small relative to the claims already outstanding cannot borrow if equity markets close, so cash-poor equity issuance by such a firm is genuinely forced, whereas a firm with plant far exceeding its liabilities always retains a secured-borrowing fallback.
considered.reasoning: The weight is now collateral measured against existing claims rather than asset composition, so it excludes cash entirely and is not contaminated by the liquidity the contrast leg subtracts — it is itself a cross-theme quantity (pledgeable investment assets versus total financing claims) and is economically distinct from the intangible-intensity predictor. It also has full continuous support across the cross-section, which the archive shows is the condition under which this architecture produces a cross-sectional slope as well as an alpha.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ErraticProgramDependence
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(VOL(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, LAG(ppent, 1)), 1), 5)), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(che, LAG(at, 1)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Outside investors cannot discipline a spending program they cannot predict: firms whose investment rate swings wildly from year to year give suppliers of capital no benchmark, so when such a firm funds itself with equity from a thin cash position the money is most likely to be misallocated, while a steady-state investor's external funding is verifiable against a stable plan.
considered.reasoning: Every conditioning weight tried so far is a level or a composition measure; this one is the second moment of the *investment* program, which is a different economic quantity from the financing volatility tested earlier (UnstablyFundedInvestment, which measured issuance instability and gave a wrong-signed alpha). It has broad continuous support by construction, and it identifies the population where monitoring is hardest rather than merely restating who invests or who issues.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: TotalFundingCapacityGap
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(capx, aqc), LAG(at, 1)), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(che, ppent), lt), at), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: A firm's true internal funding capacity is its liquid balance plus what its pledgeable assets can support net of the claims already against them; issuing equity while that whole capacity is thin is the state that reveals dependence, whereas issuing while capacity is ample is discretionary.
considered.reasoning: Rather than adding payout flows to a cash stock — the dimensionally sloppy change the critic rejected — this replaces the resource leg with a single stock-consistent measure of net pledgeable liquidity (cash plus plant less total liabilities), which brings debt capacity into the definition of internal resources for the first time in this archive. The investment-intensity weight is retained unchanged so the comparison against the existing cash-only formulation is clean, and both tails remain heavy investors.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PeakProgramFundingGap
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(RATIO(ADD(capx, aqc), LAG(at, 1)), TS_MAX(RATIO(ADD(capx, aqc), LAG(at, 1)), 5)), 1), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(che, LAG(at, 1)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Externally funded expansion is most dangerous at the top of a firm's own spending cycle, when commitments are maximal and reversal is costly; a firm running its largest program in five years on outside money from an empty balance sheet is at maximum overextension, while the same funding position at the bottom of its own cycle carries little commitment.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the positive-side self-funding construction the critic correctly noted has already failed twice and instead supplies the one weight the archive has evidence for but never implemented continuously — within-firm cycle position, which produced the strongest FMB slopes when coarsely proxied by TS_RANK and MA deviations. Expressing it as the ratio of the current program to the firm's own five-year maximum gives a bounded, continuous, firm-demeaned weight that cannot be a restatement of the cross-sectional investment level, paired with the contrast that reliably carries the FF5 alpha.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CollateralErosionDependence
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(DELTA(ppent, 1), LAG(at, 1))), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(che, LAG(at, 1)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: A firm whose tangible base is actively shrinking while it raises equity from an empty balance sheet is substituting outside capital for collateral it is losing; the direction of collateral change, not just its level, tells us whether the funding position is deteriorating.
considered.reasoning: Every conditioner tested so far is a level or a second moment; this is the first-difference version, which identifies firms whose secured-borrowing capacity is being eroded in real time — a state that the level-based headroom measure cannot see in firms that still look asset-rich. It is economically distinct from asset-growth sorts because the score is high only when shrinking collateral coincides with cash-poor issuance, and low for shrinking firms that are liquid or repurchasing.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ChronicDependenceContinuous
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(MA(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1), 3)), SUB(IND_RANK(MA(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(capx, aqc), LAG(at, 1)), 1), 3)), IND_RANK(MA(WINSOR(RATIO(che, at), 1), 3))))
considered.hypothesis: Firms that have been running programs beyond their liquid means and returning to shareholders year after year are structurally, not episodically, dependent, and that persistent state should predict returns more reliably than any single year's flows.
considered.reasoning: The three-year AND-count version of this idea produced a NaN alpha because a four-valued score cannot form stable deciles; smoothing each of the three components over three years instead preserves the persistence economics while restoring a continuous, fully rankable score. It also directly tests whether the archive's contemporaneous results are driven by transitory one-year financing events or by a durable firm state, which matters for turnover and implementability.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: UncollateralizedBorrowerDependence
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(ppent, lt)), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(dltis, dltr), LAG(at, 1)), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(che, LAG(at, 1)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Creditors normally lend against collateral, so a firm with almost no pledgeable base that is nonetheless borrowing heavily while holding no cash is being funded on unusually soft terms — the debt-market analogue of overvaluation-driven equity issuance — and should underperform just as sharply.
considered.reasoning: The entire archive's alpha engine has been built on equity issuance, and the one earlier attempt to test creditor money was rejected for anticipating a null; here the prediction is positive and theory-driven, because unsecured lending to a collateral-poor firm is precisely where creditor screening has failed. Both tails are collateral-poor firms, so the sort contrasts leveraging-up-without-collateral against deleveraging cash-rich firms rather than restating the debt-issuance effect.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PledgeabilityWithoutLeverage
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(ppent, SUB(at, che))), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(che, LAG(at, 1)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: What conditions the penalty for cash-poor equity funding is the physical pledgeability of the operating asset base, not how indebted the firm already is; a firm whose non-cash assets are mostly unpledgeable has no secured fallback regardless of its current leverage.
considered.reasoning: The critic's observation that NEG(ppent/lt) rises mechanically with total liabilities is important economically, not just cosmetically: the champion's -4.6% alpha may be a leverage-distress effect rather than a collateral effect. Scaling plant by non-cash assets purges liabilities from the weight entirely and also removes cash from the denominator, so this is a decomposition test whose outcome tells us which of two very different mechanisms the archive's best result rests on, and it keeps the champion's coverage.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: NearTermCashRequirementCoverage
considered.expression: IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(ADD(capx, aqc), ADD(dlc, dvc)), ADD(che, ppent)), 1))
considered.hypothesis: A firm's total call on cash over the coming year is its investment program plus the debt maturing plus the dividend it is expected to keep paying, and the resources it can meet that call with internally are its cash balance and the plant it could pledge or sell; when the call exceeds those resources the firm must go to the market on whatever terms are available.
considered.reasoning: This drops the weight-times-contrast architecture entirely in favour of a single coverage ratio, which removes the leverage double-count the critic identified — liabilities now appear once, in the numerator, and never in the conditioner — and eliminates the dispersion compression that multiplicative weights impose. It is also the only construction in the archive that puts investment, maturing debt and the payout commitment on the same side of a resource comparison, and its denominator uses pledgeable plant rather than cash alone, so it is not a restatement of any tested entry.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: IrreversibleProgramDependence
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, ADD(capx, ADD(aqc, ABS(DELTA(invt, 1))))), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(che, LAG(at, 1)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Externally funded expansion is most damaging when the money is sunk into assets the firm cannot walk away from: a program concentrated in fixed plant cannot be scaled back if funding dries up, whereas spending on acquisitions or inventory can be resold or run down, so irreversibility determines whether market dependence becomes a trap.
considered.reasoning: Rather than stacking two conditioners that have already been evaluated, this introduces a conditioner the archive has never used — the composition of the investment program between irreversible plant and reversible outlays — which is the standard real-options determinant of why overinvestment destroys value. The weight is a bounded composition share with broad support and no overlap with collateral, vintage, volatility or cycle position, so a result here is attributable to irreversibility rather than to a repackaging of the champion's weight.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ChronicCashRequirementCoverage
considered.expression: IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(LOG(RATIO(MA(ADD(ADD(capx, aqc), ADD(dlc, dvc)), 3), ADD(che, ppent))), 1))
considered.hypothesis: Structural dependence is revealed by a firm's sustained cash requirement, not by one year's spending: a three-year average call on cash that still exceeds today's internal resources identifies firms whose business model requires continuous market access.
considered.reasoning: Persistence and coverage have each worked separately — the three-year smoothed dependence state delivered -4.4% alpha (t -4.55) and the coverage ratio -6.1% — but the smoothed version had a flat slope while the ratio did not, so combining a smoothed need with a current resource base tests whether persistence adds information once the functional form is fixed. Averaging only the need side is deliberate: resources should be measured as they stand today, when the requirement must actually be met.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CollateralWeightedRequirementGap
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(ppent, SUB(at, che))), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(ADD(capx, aqc), ADD(dlc, dvc)), LAG(at, 1)), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(che, LAG(at, 1)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Total near-term cash requirements exceeding the liquid buffer is dangerous specifically for firms whose operating assets cannot be pledged, because those firms have no secured-borrowing fallback when equity and bond markets turn against them.
considered.reasoning: This unites the archive's two strongest families while keeping their variables in strictly disjoint roles — plant appears only in the pledgeability weight, cash only in the buffer, and the program plus contractual claims only in the need leg — which avoids the leverage and liquidity double-counting that sank earlier attempts to merge them. It replaces the champion's equity-issuance-only need leg with the full requirement measure that generated the largest alpha, so it is the batch's best candidate for joint slope and alpha strength at the archive's highest coverage.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CoverageDeterioration
considered.expression: IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(DELTA(LOG(RATIO(ADD(ADD(capx, aqc), ADD(dlc, dvc)), ADD(che, ppent))), 1), 1))
considered.hypothesis: What predicts returns is not only how dependent a firm is but whether it is becoming more so: a year in which cash requirements grew relative to internal resources marks the point at which management committed beyond its means, regardless of the starting level.
considered.reasoning: The archive has established the level of funding coverage as a powerful state variable but has never tested its first difference in a stable functional form, and the log difference is a clean growth-rate of the dependence state that is orthogonal by construction to the cross-sectional level. If it carries independent predictive content, it identifies the transition into dependence rather than the condition itself, which is a distinct economic event and a natural complement to Signal 1.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: RequirementGapWithLiquidityTrend
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(ADD(capx, aqc), ADD(dlc, dvc)), ADD(che, ppent)), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(NEG(TREND(RATIO(che, at), 3)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: A large funding requirement is tolerable for a firm that has been building liquidity year after year and dangerous for one whose liquidity has been draining, because the multi-year direction of the cash balance is the firm's demonstrated track record of generating resources internally.
considered.reasoning: Every conditioner tested so far is a contemporaneous state or a level; a multi-year liquidity trajectory is a track record, and it distinguishes firms whose requirement will be met from internal generation from those that have been running down their reserves. Both legs are non-negative ranks so the long tail remains low-requirement firms with rising liquidity — the fortress-balance-sheet population that has carried the correct side of every successful signal in this archive.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: RigidObligationsAmplifiedGap
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dlc, dvc), ADD(ADD(capx, aqc), ADD(dlc, dvc))), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(capx, aqc), LAG(at, 1)), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(che, LAG(at, 1)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: When an investment program outruns liquidity, the firm's escape route is to slow the program down — but that escape is unavailable if most of its coming-year cash calls are contractual rather than discretionary, so the same funding gap is far more damaging for a firm whose obligations are dominated by maturing debt and an established dividend.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the monotone log transform and introduces a conditioner the archive has never used — the *composition* of the cash requirement between non-deferrable claims and discretionary spending, which is the financial-flexibility determinant of whether a funding gap forces market access or merely slower growth. The variable roles are strictly disjoint: maturing debt and the dividend appear only inside the rigidity share, while the program and the cash buffer appear only in the contrast, so no term is double-counted and both tails are firms with rigid obligation structures.

considered.name: FundingQueuePosition
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(IND_ADJ(RATIO(ADD(ADD(capx, aqc), ADD(dlc, dvc)), ADD(che, ppent))), 1)), ZSCORE(SUB(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(ADD(capx, aqc), ADD(dlc, dvc)), ADD(che, ppent)), 1), IND_ADJ(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(ADD(capx, aqc), ADD(dlc, dvc)), ADD(che, ppent)), 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: Capital is allocated competitively within industries: being the worst-funded firm in an industry whose peers are all stretched means standing last in the queue for scarce external capital, whereas the same absolute funding gap in an industry where rivals are cash-rich can be financed on ordinary terms.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the anomaly bundle with a genuinely cross-level mechanism — the firm's rank within its industry's funding distribution multiplied by that industry's own average funding stress, recovered as the difference between the raw and industry-adjusted measure — so the score identifies relative position in a competition for capital rather than any single firm characteristic. It differs from the earlier hot-issuance-wave test both in the state variable (total funding coverage rather than issuance activity) and in its long tail, which is well-funded firms inside comfortable industries, the population that has carried the correct side of every successful signal in this archive.
